folder_html:
What This Shows

Expected auroral intensity and oval location over the Great Lakes from NOAA's OVATION Prime model — the same model family behind NOAA's Aurora Viewline product. Colors follow NOAA's visual concept: green auroral-oval band, warming through yellow/orange to red/magenta/violet as predicted intensity rises. This is a Google Earth raster implementation using NOAA's authoritative data, not a copy of NOAA's webpage image.

Source / Study

Product: NOAA/SWPC Aurora Viewline product family (experimental viewline page).
Model: OVATION Prime (real-time auroral precipitation model driven by solar-wind observations; forecast position/intensity of the auroral oval).
Endpoint: https://services.swpc.noaa.gov/json/ovation_aurora_latest.json
Run context: hemispheric power 40.8 GW; forecast Kp 4.
Observation time: 2026-10-10 04:21 AM EDT
Forecast time: 2026-10-10 05:24 AM EDT

How to Read the Gradient

OVATION auroral intensity, FIXED absolute scale 0–30+: LOWEST 0 (transparent, no activity) → 6 bright green (auroral oval overhead) → 14 orange → 23 magenta (severe) → HIGHEST+ 30+ (violet extreme). Same intensity always shows the same color. Model-derived viewline in basin: ~48°N (at/inside this map — northern Great Lakes may see aurora low on the northern horizon when dark) (southernmost latitude reaching intensity 5+: aurora may be visible low on the northern horizon from there under dark, clear skies).

OVATION role: OVATION converts upstream solar-wind energy into maps of auroral particle precipitation; brighter regions = stronger predicted aurora overhead.

Viewline meaning: the viewline is the southernmost region from which aurora may be seen low on the northern horizon under appropriate conditions (dark, clear, unobstructed northern view). Model-derived basin viewline now: ~48°N (at/inside this map — northern Great Lakes may see aurora low on the northern horizon when dark). Being south of the line means aurora is unlikely; being near or north of it means look north when dark — it is an opportunity boundary, not a sighting line.

Great Lakes reading: green over your lake = oval possibly overhead/near; yellow→red = strong activity nearby; violet = extreme storm conditions. Daylight, clouds, moonlight and city lights can hide even a strong forecast.

Data / Scientific Limitations

Auroral forecast/prediction only — it does not guarantee anyone will see aurora from a specific place at a specific time. Intensity is model output in OVATION units, not a naked-eye brightness meter. Coverage is the fixed project rectangle (lon −93…−73.5, lat 40.5…49.5, WGS84, 1800×1175), inherited from LIVE LEAF COLOR; it is not cropped to shorelines. Kp context supplements but never replaces the OVATION field.

Update Frequency

Source checked hourly (refreshInterval 3600 s on both the entry NetworkLink and the overlay Icon). SWPC issues new OVATION runs about every 5 minutes; the layer rebuilds only when the Observation/Forecast time actually changes (source version ovation-2026-10-10T08:21:00Z-fcst-2026-10-10T09:24:00Z).
